sec: Serum osmolality, effective osmoles and translocational hyponatremia

items.q: What is the standard formula for calculating serum osmolality?
items.exp: Serum osmolality is calculated as 2 × S.Na+ + (Blood Glucose / 18) + (BUN / 2.8). (Book p958)

items.q: What is the normal physiological reference range for serum osmolality?
items.exp: Normal serum osmolality ranges from 285 to 290 mOsm/kg of H2O. (Book p958)

items.q: Match the osmole type to its physiological behavior across cell membranes — 1) Effective osmoles (Solutes) 2) Ineffective osmoles … A) Remain confined in extracellular blood without crossing cell membrane, drawing water out of cells B) Freely cross cell membranes without generating an effective osmotic gradient
items.exp: Effective osmoles stay in blood and draw water out of cells causing hyponatremia; ineffective osmoles cross cell membranes freely. (Book p958)

items.q: Which molecule is an ineffective osmole that freely permeates cell membranes?
items.exp: Urea, ethanol, methanol, and ethylene glycol are ineffective osmoles; mannitol, glucose, and glycine are effective osmoles. (Book p958)

items.q: Tonicity represents the effective osmolality of solutes that cannot freely cross cell membranes, and is physiologically maintained predominantly by ___.
items.exp: Tonicity is effective osmolality and is governed and maintained primarily by sodium. (Book p958)

items.q: A 68-year-old male undergoes transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) with continuous bladder irrigation using a non-electrolyte glycine solution. Postoperatively, his serum sodium is 124 mEq/L while measured serum osmolality is 292 mOsm/kg. What mechanism explains this laboratory finding?
opts: Translocational pseudohyponatremia due to systemic absorption of effective solute glycine
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion triggered by surgical pain
Excessive primary renal sodium wasting from acute tubular necrosis
Psychogenic water intoxication during perioperative recovery
items.exp: Glycine is an effective solute that stays in blood without crossing cell membranes, drawing water from cells and causing translocational hyponatremia. (Book p958)

items.q: In translocational hyponatremia from hyperglycemia, for every 100 mg/dL elevation in blood glucose, serum sodium falls by approximately:
items.exp: For every 100 mg/dL rise in blood glucose, serum sodium falls by 1.6 mEq/L. (Book p958)

items.q: Match the hyponatremic state to its serum osmolality profile — 1) True hyponatremia 2) Pseudohyponatremia … A) Low serum sodium with low serum osmolality B) Low serum sodium with normal or increased serum osmolality
items.exp: True hyponatremia is low sodium with low osmolality; pseudohyponatremia features low sodium with normal or elevated osmolality. (Book p958)

items.q: Which solute is NOT listed among the effective solutes causing translocational hyponatremia?
items.exp: Glucose, mannitol, glycine, and maltose are effective solutes; ethanol is an ineffective osmole that crosses membranes freely. (Book p958)

items.q: Assess the osmotic characteristics of solutes: I Effective osmoles draw intracellular water into the vascular compartment, diluting serum sodium. II Ineffective osmoles alter effective tonicity and drive transcellular fluid shifts.
opts: Both I and II are true
Both I and II are false
items.exp: Effective osmoles cause water shifts and hyponatremia; ineffective osmoles cross membranes freely without changing effective osmolality. (Book p958)

items.q: A 50-year-old diabetic male presents with severe hyperglycemia of 700 mg/dL. His measured serum sodium is 126 mEq/L. What is his corrected serum sodium taking into account the 1.6 mEq/L correction per 100 mg/dL glucose excess above baseline (100 mg/dL)?
items.exp: Excess glucose is 600 mg/dL (6 × 100 mg/dL). Correction is 6 × 1.6 = 9.6 mEq/L. Corrected sodium = 126 + 9.6 = 135.6 mEq/L. (Book p958)

items.q: Effective solutes remain in the blood without crossing the cell membrane, drawing ___ out of cells into the intravascular space.
items.exp: Effective osmoles draw H2O out of the intracellular compartment into the blood. (Book p958)
